extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in the organization and evaluation of American universities (early 20th-century perspective)
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying the salient characteristics, types, and evaluative standards used to judge American universities and colleges (structure, finances, staff, students, facilities, governance, and academic scope). Extracts criteria and guidance for classifying and assessing institutional quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a university (modern conception)
rubrics_metrics.description: A university is defined as 'a place where the teaching that puts a man abreast of the fullest and most exact knowledge of the time is given in a range of subjects covering all the great departments of intellectual life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the benchmark for classifying institutions: by this definition not more than fifteen and possibly only ten or twelve American institutions would qualify as true universities; two-thirds of these are in the Atlantic States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private / Old type characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: The Old or Private type: a college modelled on Oxford/Cambridge with a head called the President, a number of teachers (professors), a body of governors/trustees holding property and control, a prescribed course of instruction which all students follow, dormitory buildings for student lodging, and generally effective discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such colleges are usually privately founded and often connected with a religious denomination. These institutional features are markers when evaluating an institution as of the 'private/old' type.

rubrics_metrics.name: New / Public type characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: The New or Public type: universities established, endowed, and governed by the State (usually via a Board of Regents). They commonly allow considerable freedom of course choice, have students living off-campus with little discipline, seldom have denominational affiliations, admit women, and charge very low fees for instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features distinguish state universities from private colleges and affect judgments about accessibility, curriculum breadth, and control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of faculty and external appliances
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions should have a sufficiently large staff of highly trained professors and adequate provision of laboratories, libraries, and other external appliances to teach a wide range of subjects effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an institution lacks these elements it may 'profess to teach a great variety of subjects' but will 'teach them in an imperfect way' — a key test for whether an institution truly functions as a university.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tiered classification of institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: American degree-granting bodies fall into three broad classes: (1) a small group (~10–15) of true modern universities; (2) some forty or more foundations which are close but imperfect (either limited in range or imperfect in provision); (3) a much larger third class (three hundred or more) of colleges that are, for most intents and purposes, schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria separating tiers include range of instruction, quality and training of staff, availability of graduate work, laboratories and libraries, and whether instruction meets modern university standards. Many smaller colleges would better 'renounce the privilege of granting degrees' and operate as schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenues, endowments, and funding mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly all degree-granting bodies are endowed (often by private founders or state land grants); many State universities receive annual or biennial legislative grants; a preferable plan is a permanent statute distributing a fixed fraction (a mill) of state valuation annually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private gifts frequently come with specific purposes (a complaint); broad general funds are preferable. Growing private munificence enriches major universities; some universities enjoy property tax exemptions. The stability and use of revenue materially affect institutional development and capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance structure and its effects
rubrics_metrics.description: State universities are typically controlled by a board (Regents); other institutions are governed by trustees or boards of governors (sometimes self-renewing or denominationally nominated). The president often holds a prominent role, and governance arrangements vary (board vs. faculty control).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governance affects appropriations, autonomy, and growth: enlightened legislatures/able presidents can secure liberal appropriations; hasty or unwise legislatures can cramp growth. Increasing alumni representation on governing bodies often yields better, more representative trustee selections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential authority and institutional personality
rubrics_metrics.description: The president of an American college/university typically occupies an especially prominent, sometimes almost monarchical, position relative to professors and students — more authority than European counterparts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Much depends on the individual talents and character of the president; the quality of leadership is a material factor when assessing institutional prospects and internal organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size, composition, and remuneration of the teaching staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty size and composition vary widely (examples: Harvard ~620, Yale 402, Columbia 465); salaries tend to be low relative to national wealth and living costs (few exceed $5,000–7,000; many professors and presidents earn far less).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate numbers of well-trained professors (including those trained abroad) are crucial for high-quality instruction and research. Low salaries are noted but do not fully prevent the presence of many able men attracted by interest in learning or religious motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility and socio-economic composition of students
rubrics_metrics.description: American universities are notably accessible to all classes. Eastern institutions admit some sons of working men; Western State universities often make little or no charge and receive students from diverse economic backgrounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic accessibility (low fees, charitable funds, opportunities for students to earn support) is a positive evaluative criterion. Differences in regional composition (East vs West) and the role of preparatory departments should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student age, course duration, and mobility
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical entrant age at leading Eastern universities is 18–19, graduation at 22–23 for a regular four-year course; Western students often enter older (24–25). Students often complete four years at the same institution though some move to larger universities for professional or postgraduate study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Age profiles, standard course length, and pathways to professional/graduate schools are indicators of institutional role and student preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buildings, campus layout, and external aspect
rubrics_metrics.description: Few college buildings are over a century old; many newer ones are handsome but there is criticism of excessive spending on showy buildings (especially in the West). Campus plans rarely use quadrangles; detached buildings are preferred for climate reasons. Attractive grounds and planting (e.g., elms) contribute positively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical plant should be judged for suitability and contribution to academic life rather than merely show. Campus situation and grounds (pleasant surroundings, adequate infrastructure) are part of institutional quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic calendar and time spent in study
rubrics_metrics.description: Vacations in American universities are shorter than in England or Scotland; the summer vacation usually lasts from the middle of June to the middle or end of September.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length of vacation and academic calendar influence time spent in study and intensity of instruction; shorter vacations imply a denser academic year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency of state funding to favor practical branches
rubrics_metrics.description: State legislatures have recently shown growing interest in university work but are 'too apt to bestow their liberality almost wholly on the more directly practical branches of its work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a state-funded university, consider potential funding biases toward practical or vocational programs at the expense of broader scholarly fields; this can shape institutional priorities and curricula.
